```{r}
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
```

# Data from Web Pages {#sec-web}

Much of the information an auditor needs is published on the internet, and only there. A state e-procurement portal lists every tender, with the date it was published and the date it closed. It also shows who won each contract, and at what value. A department publishes the list of firms it has debarred. A price portal shows the rates notified for cement or medicines. None of this comes to us as a file. It is spread over web pages, ten or twenty rows to a page.

Yet these pages answer real audit questions. Was a tender really published for the required number of days, or only for a week? Is the contract value in the division's register the same as the value the portal shows? Has the division paid a firm that the State had already debarred? To answer them, we must compare the auditee's records with what was published. Copying a few hundred rows from a website by hand is slow, and it brings typing errors. R can read the pages for us. This is called **web scraping**.

In this chapter we learn to do it with the package `rvest`.

- What a web page is made of, and how to look at its structure with the browser's **Inspect** tool.
- Reading a page, and picking out its parts with **CSS selectors**.
- Taking text, links and tables out of a page, and cleaning them into dates and amounts.
- Reading many pages one after another, and following links to detail pages.
- Two audit use cases, on the time tenders were kept open and on payments to debarred firms.
- Keeping a dated copy of the pages as audit evidence, and scraping a real website responsibly.

The book does not depend on any live website. Websites change, they may block programs, and copying a real portal's pages raises questions of permission. So we use a small **mock website** made for this book, saved as plain HTML files in the folder `Data/web`. It imitates the e-procurement portal of an imaginary "Example State". Every name on it is made up. The methods are exactly those we would use on a real site.

**Prerequisites**

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(tidyverse)
library(rvest)   # reading and taking apart web pages
```

`rvest` is installed with `install.packages("rvest")`. It also installs `xml2`, which does the actual reading of HTML.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Packages for this chapter

This chapter uses `httr2`, `rvest`, `stringdist`, `tidyverse` and `xml2`. If any of them is missing, install them with the command below. @sec-packages-install lists the packages of every part.

```r
install.packages(c("httr2", "rvest", "stringdist", "tidyverse", "xml2"))
```
:::

## Our data, a mock e-procurement portal and two registers {#sec-web-data}

We are auditing the Public Works Department (PWD), Amarpur Division, of Example State. The audit covers the tenders the division invited and the payments it made from April to November 2024. The State's e-procurement portal is our independent source. Its pages, as they stood on 2 December 2024, are saved in `Data/web`.

```{r}
list.files("Data/web")
```

- `tenders-page1.html`, `tenders-page2.html` and `tenders-page3.html` list the active tenders of all departments, six to a page, with a "Next" link at the foot of each page.
- The three `award-...html` pages give the award details of the tenders marked "Awarded". They are reached by a link in the tender list.
- `debarred-firms.html` is the State's list of debarred firms, with the period of debarment.
- `robots.txt` is the file in which a website states which parts programs may visit. We meet it in @sec-web-real.

Open `Data/web/tenders-page1.html` in a browser (double-click it in the file explorer). It looks like a simple government portal, with a blue header, a menu and a table.

From the division we have two registers. The **tender register** lists the tenders the division says it invited, with the date of the notice inviting tender (NIT), the closing date and, for awarded works, the contract value. The **payment register** lists the payments made to contractors and suppliers. The code below creates both, with a few problems planted in them. It also defines `inr()`, a small helper that writes an amount with Indian commas, for use in the text.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code to create the tender register and the payment register"
# Write an amount with Indian commas, like 12,45,000
inr <- function(x) {
  s <- format(round(x), scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
  n <- nchar(s)
  if (n <= 3) return(s)
  head <- gsub("(\\d)(?=(\\d{2})+$)", "\\1,", substr(s, 1, n - 3), perl = TRUE)
  paste0(head, ",", substr(s, n - 2, n))
}

tender_register <- tribble(
  ~tender_id,     ~work,                                      ~nit_date,    ~closing_date, ~contract_value,
  "2024_PWD_131", "CC road, Ward 7, Amarpur",                 "2024-11-18", "2024-12-09",  NA,
  "2024_PWD_129", "Repair of Tehsil office, Amarpur",         "2024-10-25", "2024-11-20",  NA,
  "2024_PWD_126", "Boundary wall, Girls School, Rampur",      "2024-11-04", "2024-11-25",  NA,
  "2024_PWD_124", "Approach road to Mandi, Belapur",          "2024-10-29", "2024-11-19",  NA,
  "2024_PWD_122", "Widening of Amarpur Belapur road",         "2024-10-25", "2024-11-15",  NA,
  "2024_PWD_119", "Community hall, Fatehpur",                 "2024-10-17", "2024-10-29",  NA,
  "2024_PWD_117", "Drain along Station Road, Amarpur",        "2024-10-09", "2024-10-30",  NA,
  "2024_PWD_114", "Resurfacing of Civil Lines roads",         "2024-09-26", "2024-10-16",  6185000,
  "2024_PWD_111", "Culvert at km 12, Belapur road",           "2024-09-11", "2024-10-02",  1972400,
  "2024_PWD_108", "Rain shelter at bus stand, Rampur",        "2024-09-02", "2024-09-23",  812600
) |>
  mutate(across(c(nit_date, closing_date), ymd))
# Planted. 2024_PWD_129 shows an NIT date two weeks earlier than the portal does
# Planted. 2024_PWD_124 is in the register but was never published on the portal
# Planted. The contract value of 2024_PWD_111 is Rs 1 lakh more than the portal shows

set.seed(2024)
regular_firms <- c("Sharma Traders", "Gupta and Sons", "Kaveri Infra Projects",
                   "Bharat Stationers", "Laxmi Electricals", "Patel Hardware")
ordinary <- tibble(
  payment_date = as.Date("2024-04-01") + sample(0:243, 40, replace = TRUE),
  payee        = sample(regular_firms, 40, replace = TRUE),
  amount       = round(runif(40, 20000, 900000), -2)
)
planted <- tribble(
  ~payment_date, ~payee,                              ~amount,
  "2024-05-14",  "Shivam Constructions Pvt. Ltd.",    412500,  # before its debarment
  "2024-08-22",  "M/s Shivam Constructions Pvt Ltd",  685000,  # after its debarment
  "2024-10-03",  "Shivam Constructions (P) Ltd",      238400,  # after its debarment
  "2024-10-18",  "Vinayak Buildcon",                  547800,  # spelt differently, after debarment
  "2024-06-11",  "R K Electricals and Co",             96500,  # before its debarment began
  "2024-07-09",  "Maa Durga Suppliers",               152300   # after its debarment ended
) |>
  mutate(payment_date = ymd(payment_date))

payments <- bind_rows(ordinary, planted) |>
  arrange(payment_date) |>
  mutate(voucher_no = sprintf("PWD/AMR/%03d", row_number()), .before = 1)
```

```{r}
tender_register
glimpse(payments)
```

The tender register has `r nrow(tender_register)` tenders, and the payment register has `r nrow(payments)` payments worth ₹`r round(sum(payments$amount) / 1e5, 1)` lakh.

## What a web page is {#sec-web-html}

A web page is a text file written in **HTML** (HyperText Markup Language). The browser reads the file and draws the page. The text is marked up with **tags** in angle brackets. Most tags come in pairs, an opening tag like `<p>` and a closing tag like `</p>`, with the content in between. Together they make an **element**.

Here are the tags we meet most often.

| Tag | What it holds |
|-----------|-----------------------------------------------|
| `<h1>`, `<h2>` | Headings |
| `<p>` | A paragraph of text |
| `<a href="...">` | A link. The address it points to is in `href` |
| `<ul>`, `<li>` | A list, and an item of the list |
| `<table>`, `<tr>`, `<th>`, `<td>` | A table, a row, a header cell and a data cell |
| `<div>`, `<span>` | Containers used to group things, for layout |

An opening tag may carry **attributes**, written as `name="value"`. Two attributes matter most for scraping. The `class` attribute puts an element in a named group, such as `class="amount"`, usually so that the page can style all amounts alike. The `id` attribute gives an element a name that is unique on the page, such as `id="tender-list"`. Elements sit inside other elements, like boxes inside boxes. A `<td>` is inside a `<tr>`, which is inside a `<table>`.

Let us make a tiny page with `minimal_html()`, which turns a piece of HTML in a string into a page R can read.

```{r}
tiny <- minimal_html('
  <h2>Notice board</h2>
  <p class="notice">Pre-bid meeting on <b>12-Nov-2024</b> at 11:00</p>
  <p class="notice">Last date extended to <b>29-Nov-2024</b></p>
  <a class="doc" href="nit-2024-131.pdf">Download NIT</a>
  <table>
    <tr><th>Item</th><th>Rate</th></tr>
    <tr><td>Cement (bag)</td><td>420</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Steel (quintal)</td><td>6,150</td></tr>
  </table>')
tiny
```

To get something out of a page, we take two steps. First we **select** the elements we want. Then we **extract** what we need from them. That may be their text, an attribute, or a whole table.

```{r}
# all elements with class "notice", and their text
tiny |> html_elements(".notice") |> html_text2()

# the address the link points to
tiny |> html_element("a.doc") |> html_attr("href")

# the table, as a tibble
tiny |> html_element("table") |> html_table()
```

That is the whole of web scraping in miniature. The rest of the chapter is about choosing the right elements on real pages, and cleaning what comes out.

## Looking inside a page with Inspect {#sec-web-inspect}

To select elements, we must know how the page is built. Every modern browser can show this. Open `tenders-page1.html` in Chrome, Edge or Firefox, right-click on a tender amount and choose **Inspect**. A panel opens beside the page, showing the HTML, with the element we clicked highlighted.

```html
<tr><td>1</td><td class="tender-id">2024_PWD_131</td>
    <td class="title">Construction of CC road, Ward 7, Amarpur</td>
    ...
    <td class="amount">&#8377; 48,60,000.00</td>
    <td class="status">Open</td></tr>
```

Move the mouse over the lines in the panel. The browser shades the part of the page each line draws. In a few minutes we can learn the plan of the page. Here, each tender is a row `<tr>` of the table with `id="tender-list"`. Each cell has a class that names its content, such as `tender-id`, `published`, `closing` or `amount`. The "Next" link has `class="next"`. (`&#8377;` is the code for the rupee sign `₹`.)

We then write **CSS selectors**, short patterns that pick elements. They are the same patterns web designers use to style pages. These few cover most needs.

| Selector | Picks |
|----------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| `td` | Every element with the tag `td` |
| `.amount` | Every element with `class="amount"` |
| `#tender-list` | The element with `id="tender-list"` |
| `td.amount` | Every `td` with `class="amount"` |
| `#tender-list tbody tr` | Every `tr` inside a `tbody` inside the element `#tender-list` (a space means "somewhere inside") |
| `a[href]` | Every link that has an `href` attribute |
| `a.next` | The link with `class="next"` |

In the Inspect panel, right-click an element and choose **Copy**, then **Copy selector**, to get a selector the browser writes for us. It is often long and fragile, like `body > main > table > tbody > tr:nth-child(3) > td:nth-child(7)`. A short selector built on a meaningful `id` or `class`, like `td.amount`, is better, because it still works when a row is added or the layout changes a little.

::: callout-tip
## Audit tip

Before writing any code, spend five minutes with Inspect on two or three pages of the site. Note the `id` of the table, the classes of the cells, how the "Next" link is marked, and whether detail pages have the same plan. Write these down in the working papers, with the date. If the site changes later, this note explains why the old code no longer works.
:::

## Reading a page with rvest {#sec-web-rvest}

`read_html()` reads a page. It takes a file path or a web address. Here it is a file on our disk.

```{r}
page1 <- read_html("Data/web/tenders-page1.html")
page1
```

`html_element()` (singular) gives the **first** matching element. `html_elements()` (plural) gives **all** of them. `html_text2()` gives the text as a browser would show it, with extra spaces and line breaks tidied.

```{r}
page1 |> html_element("h2") |> html_text2()
page1 |> html_element("p.generated") |> html_text2()
page1 |> html_elements("td.tender-id") |> html_text2()
```

`html_attr()` gives the value of an attribute. The links of the menu, for example.

```{r}
menu <- page1 |> html_elements("nav a")
tibble(text = html_text2(menu), link = html_attr(menu, "href"))
```

### A whole table with `html_table()`

When the data sits in a proper `<table>`, `html_table()` reads it in one step.

```{r}
page1 |> html_element("#tender-list") |> html_table()
```

That is quick, and it is enough for many pages. But note what it lost. The status "Awarded" in the table is a link to the award details, and `html_table()` keeps only the text, not the address. When we need links, we read the table row by row.

### Row by row, keeping the links

We select the rows, and then, *from each row*, the cell we want. Here the difference between `html_element()` and `html_elements()` matters. Applied to a set of rows, `html_element()` returns exactly one result for each row, and `NA` where the row has no such element. So the columns of our table always line up, even though only some rows have an award link.

```{r}
rows <- page1 |> html_elements("#tender-list tbody tr")
length(rows)

tibble(
  tender_id  = rows |> html_element("td.tender-id") |> html_text2(),
  status     = rows |> html_element("td.status") |> html_text2(),
  award_link = rows |> html_element("a.award-link") |> html_attr("href")
)
```

Had we used `html_elements()` for the links, we would have got only the links that exist, with no way to tell which row each came from.

## Cleaning scraped text {#sec-web-clean}

Everything taken from a web page is text. Dates come as "18-Nov-2024 10:00" and amounts as "₹ 48,60,000.00". Before any analysis we turn them into proper types. Let us write one function that reads a tender page into a clean table. We will reuse it for every page.

```{r}
read_tender_page <- function(file) {
  rows <- read_html(file) |> html_elements("#tender-list tbody tr")
  tibble(
    tender_id   = rows |> html_element("td.tender-id") |> html_text2(),
    title       = rows |> html_element("td.title") |> html_text2(),
    org         = rows |> html_element("td.org") |> html_text2(),
    published   = rows |> html_element("td.published") |> html_text2(),
    closing     = rows |> html_element("td.closing") |> html_text2(),
    value       = rows |> html_element("td.amount") |> html_text2(),
    status      = rows |> html_element("td.status") |> html_text2(),
    award_link  = rows |> html_element("a.award-link") |> html_attr("href"),
    source_file = basename(file)
  ) |>
    mutate(published = dmy_hm(published, tz = "Asia/Kolkata"),
           closing   = dmy_hm(closing, tz = "Asia/Kolkata"),
           value     = parse_number(value))
}

read_tender_page("Data/web/tenders-page1.html") |>
  select(tender_id, published, closing, value)
```

Two functions did the cleaning.

- `dmy_hm()` from `lubridate` (@sec-lubridate) reads a date written day first, with the month as a word, followed by hours and minutes. We give the time zone `"Asia/Kolkata"`, since the portal shows Indian time.
- `parse_number()` from `readr` (@sec-read-check) drops the rupee sign and the commas and keeps the number. It does not care where the commas are, so Indian grouping like "1,24,50,000" is read correctly as `r format(parse_number("1,24,50,000"), big.mark = "", scientific = FALSE)`.

We also kept `source_file`, so that every row can be traced back to the page it came from.

::: callout-warning
## Caution

`parse_number()` reads the *first* number it finds in the text. A cell like "₹ 12.5 lakh" becomes 12.5, not 12,50,000. A cell like "Rs. 5,00,000" gives `NA` with a warning, because the full stop after "Rs" confuses it. Remove such prefixes first, for example with `str_remove(x, "Rs\\.?")`. Look at a sample of the raw text before trusting the conversion, and check how many values came out as `NA`. Dates need the same care. A page may show "02/12/2024" on one screen and "2-Dec-24" on another.
:::

## Many pages, one after another {#sec-web-pages}

A portal rarely shows everything on one page. Ours shows six tenders to a page, with a "Next" link. There are two ways to read all the pages.

**When the addresses follow a pattern.** Our pages are `tenders-page1.html` to `tenders-page3.html`. On real portals the pattern is often in the address itself, like `.../tenders?page=2`. We build the addresses with `paste0()`, read each with `map()` (@sec-purrr), and stack the results with `list_rbind()`.

```{r}
page_files <- paste0("Data/web/tenders-page", 1:3, ".html")
tenders <- page_files |>
  map(read_tender_page) |>
  list_rbind()
tenders |> count(source_file)
```

**When we only know the first page.** Then we follow the "Next" link until there is none. `url_absolute()` turns a link like `"tenders-page2.html"` into a full address, by joining it to the address of the page it was found on.

```{r}
current <- "Data/web/tenders-page1.html"
visited <- character()
while (!is.na(current)) {
  visited <- c(visited, current)
  next_link <- read_html(current) |> html_element("a.next") |> html_attr("href")
  current <- if (is.na(next_link)) NA else url_absolute(next_link, current)
}
visited
```

The loop stops on the last page, which has no "Next" link. On a real website, add a pause with `Sys.sleep()` inside the loop and a limit on the number of pages, so that a fault in the site can never send the program round and round (@sec-web-real).

### Did we get everything?

A scrape that silently misses a page is worse than no scrape. Each page of our portal states the total number of tenders found. Let us compare it with what we read, and check for repeated rows and missing values.

```{r}
total_on_site <- page1 |> html_element("p.total") |> html_text2() |> parse_number()

tenders |>
  summarise(rows_read = n(),
            total_on_site = total_on_site,
            distinct_ids = n_distinct(tender_id),
            missing_dates = sum(is.na(published) | is.na(closing)),
            missing_values = sum(is.na(value)))
```

We read `r nrow(tenders)` tenders, the site says `r total_on_site`, every tender ID is distinct, and nothing is missing. The scrape is complete.

## Following links to detail pages {#sec-web-links}

Of the `r nrow(tenders)` tenders, `r sum(!is.na(tenders$award_link))` are marked "Awarded", and each has a link to a page of award details. Let us open one.

```{r}
award_page <- read_html("Data/web/award-2024_PWD_111.html")
award_page |> html_element("table") |> html_table()
```

This table is laid out with labels in the first column and values in the second. We read each award page into one row with a small function. It uses `pivot_wider()` (@sec-tidyr) to turn the labels into column names.

```{r}
read_award_page <- function(file) {
  read_html(file) |>
    html_element("table.award-details") |>
    html_table(header = FALSE) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = X1, values_from = X2)
}

award_files <- tenders |>
  filter(!is.na(award_link)) |>
  mutate(file = url_absolute(award_link, "Data/web/tenders-page1.html")) |>
  pull(file)
award_files

awards <- award_files |>
  map(read_award_page) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  transmute(tender_id      = `Tender ID`,
            bids           = as.integer(`Number of Bids Received`),
            awarded_to     = `Awarded To`,
            portal_value   = parse_number(`Contract Value`),
            award_date     = dmy(`Date of Award`))
awards
```

Now the portal can be compared with the division's tender register, with a join (@sec-joins).

```{r}
value_check <- tender_register |>
  inner_join(awards, by = "tender_id") |>
  mutate(difference = contract_value - portal_value) |>
  select(tender_id, awarded_to, contract_value, portal_value, difference)
value_check
```

```{r}
#| include: false
diff_row <- value_check |> filter(difference != 0)
```

For `r diff_row$tender_id`, awarded to `r diff_row$awarded_to`, the register shows a contract value of ₹`r inr(diff_row$contract_value)`. The portal shows ₹`r inr(diff_row$portal_value)`, which is ₹`r inr(diff_row$difference)` less. The auditor should see the agreement and the letter of award. If the agreement was signed for more than the awarded value, the division must explain why, and whether it was approved.

## Audit use case, were tenders open long enough? {#sec-web-days}

A tender must stay open long enough for every interested firm to see it and prepare a bid. A short window favours a firm that knew about the work in advance, and reduces competition. In our example, suppose the procurement rules of Example State require at least **21 days** from publication on the portal to the closing date. (This is an example norm for our imaginary state. The auditor must apply the norm that actually governs the auditee, which may differ with the type and value of the tender.)

We compute the days each tender was open, from the date of publication to the date of closing, and flag those below the norm.

```{r}
min_days <- 21
short_window <- tenders |>
  mutate(days_open = as.numeric(as_date(closing) - as_date(published))) |>
  filter(days_open < min_days) |>
  select(tender_id, org, published, closing, days_open, value)
short_window
```

```{r}
#| include: false
sw <- short_window |> arrange(days_open)
```

In all, `r nrow(short_window)` tenders were open for fewer than `r min_days` days, all of them of the PWD, Amarpur Division. `r sw$tender_id[1]` was open for only `r sw$days_open[1]` days. `r sw$tender_id[3]` was open for `r sw$days_open[3]` days, just one day short. A shortfall of one day is easy to miss by eye, and that is exactly why a computed check is useful.

Now let us bring in the division's own tender register. Two more questions arise. Is every tender in the register on the portal at all? And do the dates in the register agree with the portal?

```{r}
# tenders in the register that the portal does not show
not_on_portal <- tender_register |> anti_join(tenders, by = "tender_id")
not_on_portal

# NIT dates in the register that differ from the date of publication on the portal
date_check <- tender_register |>
  inner_join(tenders |> select(tender_id, published), by = "tender_id") |>
  mutate(portal_date = as_date(published),
         days_apart  = as.numeric(nit_date - portal_date)) |>
  filter(days_apart != 0) |>
  select(tender_id, nit_date, portal_date, days_apart, closing_date)
date_check
```

The results tell a clear story.

- `r not_on_portal$tender_id`, "`r not_on_portal$work`", is in the register but was never published on the portal. A tender that was not published was not open to competition at all.
- For `r date_check$tender_id`, the register gives the NIT date as `r format(date_check$nit_date, "%d %B %Y")`. The portal shows it was published only on `r format(date_check$portal_date, "%d %B %Y")`. By the register, the tender was open for `r as.numeric(date_check$closing_date - date_check$nit_date)` days and met the norm. By the portal, it was open for `r short_window$days_open[short_window$tender_id == date_check$tender_id]` days. The register appears to have been written to hide the short window.

**What the auditor does next.** Call for the tender files of the `r nrow(short_window) + nrow(not_on_portal)` tenders. See whether a shorter period was approved, by whom and for what reason, as many rules allow in a real emergency. Count the bids received in each, since a short window often goes with a single bid. Ask how the unpublished tender was awarded. And ask the division to explain the NIT date in its register.

## Audit use case, payments to debarred firms {#sec-web-debarred}

A debarred firm must not be given any work during the period of its debarment. Payments to such a firm, for work given during that period, show that the division did not check the list. Let us read the list from the portal. It is a plain table, so `html_table()` is enough.

```{r}
debarred <- read_html("Data/web/debarred-firms.html") |>
  html_element("#debarred") |>
  html_table() |>
  transmute(firm = `Name of Firm`,
            from = dmy(`Debarred From`),
            to   = dmy(`Debarred Up To`),
            order_no = `Order No.`)
debarred
```

### Cleaning the names before matching

The names on the portal and in the payment register are written differently. One has "SHIVAM CONSTRUCTIONS PRIVATE LIMITED", the other "Shivam Constructions Pvt. Ltd.". An exact join would find no match at all. So we first bring both to a common form, as in @sec-strng. We change to capitals, remove "M/s" and "(P)", write "&" as "AND", drop punctuation, and drop words like "Private", "Limited" and "Co" that say nothing about who the firm is.

```{r}
clean_firm <- function(x) {
  x |>
    str_to_upper() |>
    str_remove("^M/S\\.?\\s*") |>
    str_remove_all("\\(P\\)") |>
    str_replace_all("&", " AND ") |>
    str_replace_all("[[:punct:]]", " ") |>
    str_squish() |>
    str_remove_all("\\b(PRIVATE|PVT|LIMITED|LTD|AND CO|CO)\\b") |>
    str_squish()
}

tibble(original = c("SHIVAM CONSTRUCTIONS PRIVATE LIMITED", "M/s Shivam Constructions Pvt Ltd",
                    "Shivam Constructions (P) Ltd", "R. K. ELECTRICALS & CO.")) |>
  mutate(cleaned = clean_firm(original))
```

Now we match the cleaned names, and then check the dates. A payment is a concern only if it falls within the period of debarment.

```{r}
debarred <- debarred |> mutate(name_key = clean_firm(firm))
payments <- payments |> mutate(name_key = clean_firm(payee))

name_matches <- payments |>
  inner_join(debarred, by = "name_key") |>
  mutate(in_period = payment_date >= from & payment_date <= to) |>
  select(voucher_no, payment_date, payee, amount, firm, from, to, in_period)
name_matches
```

```{r}
#| include: false
out_period <- name_matches |> filter(!in_period)
in_period  <- name_matches |> filter(in_period)
```

After cleaning, `r nrow(name_matches)` payments match firms on the debarred list. But `r nrow(out_period)` of them were made outside the period of debarment. The first payment to Shivam Constructions was made before its debarment began on 1 July 2024. The payment to R K Electricals came before its debarment from 1 December 2024. Maa Durga Suppliers was paid after its debarment had ended in January 2024. These are not findings. Only the `r nrow(in_period)` payments to Shivam Constructions in August and October 2024 fall inside the period.

### Names that cleaning does not catch

Cleaning removes differences of case, punctuation and legal form. It does not catch a name spelt differently, like "Vinayak Buildcon" for "Vinayaka Build Con". For these we compare the names that did not match with every debarred name, and look at the closest ones. The Jaro-Winkler distance from `stringdist` (@sec-strsim) is 0 for identical strings and grows towards 1 as they differ. We remove the spaces first, so that "BUILD CON" and "BUILDCON" are compared fairly.

```{r}
unmatched <- payments |>
  anti_join(debarred, by = "name_key") |>
  distinct(payee, name_key)

near_matches <- cross_join(unmatched, debarred |> select(firm, name_key, from, to),
                           suffix = c("_paid", "_debarred")) |>
  mutate(distance = stringdist::stringdist(str_remove_all(name_key_paid, " "),
                                           str_remove_all(name_key_debarred, " "),
                                           method = "jw", p = 0.1)) |>
  filter(distance < 0.1) |>
  arrange(distance)
near_matches |> select(payee, firm, distance)
```

Only one pair is close. The cut-off of 0.1 is a judgement, and every pair it finds must be checked by a person, as @sec-strsim explains. For a large list, the steps of @sec-linkage make such matching more reliable. Let us take the payments of this firm and check the period.

```{r}
fuzzy_hits <- payments |>
  inner_join(near_matches |> select(payee, firm, from, to), by = "payee") |>
  filter(payment_date >= from, payment_date <= to) |>
  select(voucher_no, payment_date, payee, amount, firm, from, to)
fuzzy_hits
```

```{r}
#| include: false
findings <- bind_rows(in_period |> select(voucher_no, payee, amount),
                      fuzzy_hits |> select(voucher_no, payee, amount))
```

In all, `r nrow(findings)` payments worth ₹`r inr(sum(findings$amount))` were made to firms during their debarment. Of these, `r nrow(fuzzy_hits)` would have been missed by an exact match, even after cleaning.

**What the auditor does next.** For each of these payments, see when the work was given to the firm. A payment during debarment for work given *before* it may be in order under the rules, while work given during debarment is not. Find out whether the division checked the debarred list before awarding the work. And confirm that "Vinayak Buildcon" is the same firm as "Vinayaka Build Con", from the PAN, GST number or bank account in the firm's papers, before reporting it.

## Keeping evidence of what was collected {#sec-web-evidence}

::: callout-warning
## Caution

Scraped data is only as good as the page it came from, and web pages change. A tender may be corrected, a firm removed from the debarred list, or the whole portal redesigned. If the auditee later disputes a finding, "the website showed it" is not evidence unless we can show *what* it showed and *when*. So, for every scrape, record the address of each page and the date and time of collection, and save a copy of each page exactly as received, in the working papers.
:::

The best copy is the file exactly as the server sent it. For our mock site we simply copy the files into a folder named with the date. On a real site, `req_perform(path = ...)` of `httr2` saves the page straight to a file (@sec-web-real). We also record a **checksum** of each file with `tools::md5sum()`. If even one character of a saved page is changed later, its checksum changes, so the log proves the copy is the one we collected.

```{r}
evidence_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), paste0("web-evidence-", format(Sys.Date(), "%Y-%m-%d")))
dir.create(evidence_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

sources <- c(page_files, award_files, "Data/web/debarred-firms.html")
copies  <- file.path(evidence_dir, basename(sources))
file.copy(sources, copies, overwrite = TRUE) |> all()

evidence_log <- tibble(
  source       = sources,
  saved_as     = basename(copies),
  collected_at = format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %Z"),
  md5          = unname(tools::md5sum(copies))
)
evidence_log |> select(saved_as, md5)
```

When we have only the parsed page in R, `write_html()` from `xml2` writes it back to a file. This keeps the content, though not always the exact bytes of the original.

```{r}
xml2::write_html(page1, file.path(evidence_dir, "tenders-page1-parsed.html"))
```

Save the evidence log as a CSV beside the copies, and run the analysis on the saved copies, not on the live site. Then the analysis can be run again at any time, by anyone, and gives the same result. @sec-reports shows how to organise such files in an audit project.

## Scraping a real website responsibly {#sec-web-real}

Everything above works on a real website by giving `read_html()` a web address instead of a file. But a real website belongs to someone, and runs on a server that others need too. A scraper sends requests much faster than a person clicking. Careless scraping can slow a site down for everyone, break its terms of use, or be blocked as an attack. An auditor must be beyond reproach here. Follow these rules.

1. **Look for an official source first.** Many portals offer a download in Excel or CSV, an open data page, or an API (a service that gives data to programs). Ask the department or the portal's owner for the data. Scrape only if there is no better way.
2. **Read the site's terms of use and its `robots.txt`.** The file `robots.txt`, at the root of a site, says which parts programs may not visit, and sometimes how long to wait between requests. Respect both.
3. **Identify yourself.** Send a "user agent" that names your office and gives a contact address, so the site's owner knows who is visiting and why.
4. **Go slowly.** Wait a few seconds between requests, and never send requests in parallel. Scrape outside office hours, when fewer people need the site.
5. **Never log in or break any barrier.** Do not use anyone's password, do not try to get round a CAPTCHA, a login page or a block, and do not visit pages that are not open to the public. If the data is behind a login, ask for it officially.
6. **Take only what you need, once.** Save the pages (@sec-web-evidence) and work on the copies, rather than reading the site again and again.

Here is the `robots.txt` of our mock portal.

```{r}
readLines("Data/web/robots.txt")
```

It asks programs not to visit the `bidder` and `admin` sections, and to wait 10 seconds between requests. The "Bidder Login" link in the portal's menu leads into the `bidder` section, so our scraper must never follow it.

The code below shows how a polite scraper of a real portal may look. It is not run in this book, and the address `https://eprocure.example.gov.in` is a placeholder, not a real portal. It uses `httr2`, which gives more control than `read_html()` alone. `req_user_agent()` identifies us, `req_throttle()` limits the rate of requests, `req_retry()` tries again a few times if the server is busy, and `req_perform(path = ...)` saves each page to a file. The pause with `Sys.sleep()` keeps us well within the 10 seconds the site asked for.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(httr2)

base_url <- "https://eprocure.example.gov.in"   # placeholder, not a real portal

# 1. Read the site's rules first
request(base_url) |>
  req_url_path("robots.txt") |>
  req_perform() |>
  resp_body_string() |>
  cat()

# 2. A polite request, that names us and goes slowly
polite_request <- function(url) {
  request(url) |>
    req_user_agent("Audit team, Office of the Accountant General, Example State (audit.team@example.gov.in)") |>
    req_throttle(rate = 5 / 60) |>        # at most 5 requests a minute
    req_retry(max_tries = 3) |>
    req_timeout(60)
}

# 3. Save each page, as received, in a dated folder
evidence_dir <- file.path("evidence", paste0("eprocure-", format(Sys.Date(), "%Y-%m-%d")))
dir.create(evidence_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

urls  <- paste0(base_url, "/tenders?page=", 1:3)
files <- file.path(evidence_dir, paste0("tenders-page", 1:3, ".html"))
for (i in seq_along(urls)) {
  polite_request(urls[i]) |> req_perform(path = files[i])
  Sys.sleep(15)                           # a pause between pages
}

# 4. Analyse the saved copies, exactly as in this chapter
tenders <- files |> map(read_tender_page) |> list_rbind()
```

::: callout-note
Some websites build their pages with JavaScript after they load. `read_html()` then gets only an empty frame, without the table we see in the browser. Open Inspect, go to the **Network** tab and reload the page. Often the data arrives from an API as JSON, which `httr2` can read with `resp_body_json()`, after checking that the site allows it. `rvest` also has `read_html_live()`, which runs a real browser in the background. Use these only on public pages, and with the same care.
:::

## A suggested workflow

1. **Look for a better source.** An official download, an API, or a request to the department.
2. **Read the rules of the site.** Its terms of use and `robots.txt`. Note them in the working papers.
3. **Study the page with Inspect.** Find the `id` of the table, the classes of the cells and the "Next" link, and choose short, meaningful CSS selectors.
4. **Save the pages first.** Politely, with a user agent and pauses, into a dated folder, with an evidence log of addresses, times and checksums.
5. **Read the saved copies.** Write one function for one page, using `html_elements()` for rows and `html_element()` for the cells in each row, then `map()` it over all the pages.
6. **Clean the text.** Dates with `dmy_hm()` or `dmy()`, amounts with `parse_number()`, and names with a cleaning function.
7. **Check completeness.** Compare the rows read with the total the site shows, and look for repeats and `NA`s.
8. **Compare with the auditee's records.** Join on IDs and cleaned names, test dates against the norm, and confirm every hit from the documents before reporting it.

::: callout-important
## Remember

- A web page is HTML. Tags make elements, and the `class` and `id` attributes help us select them with CSS selectors.
- `read_html()` reads a page, `html_elements()` and `html_element()` select, and `html_text2()`, `html_attr()` and `html_table()` extract.
- Select the rows first, then one cell from each row with `html_element()`, so that the columns line up.
- Read many pages with `map()`, or by following the "Next" link, and check that the count matches the site.
- Scraped data is evidence only if we record where and when it was collected, and keep a copy.
- On real sites, prefer an official source, respect the rules, identify yourself, go slowly, and never log in or get round a barrier.
:::

## Where next

The checks in this chapter rest on joins, covered in @sec-joins, and on dates, covered in @sec-lubridate. For cleaning names and matching them when they are spelt differently, see @sec-strng, @sec-strsim and @sec-linkage. For data that arrives as PDF or awkward Excel files, see @sec-pdfxl. @sec-reports shows how to keep the saved pages, the evidence log and the analysis together as working papers.

## Try it yourself {#sec-web-exercises}

These exercises use the pages of the mock portal in `Data/web`, and the tables we built from them in this chapter, `tenders`, `awards`, `tender_register` and `payments`. No real website is needed. Try each one before you open the solution. Some solutions use dplyr verbs such as `anti_join()`, `arrange()` and `filter()`, which @sec-DPLYRR and @sec-joins explain in full.

1.  **A shorter norm.** Suppose the rules allowed only 14 days for urgent works. Which tenders would fall short even of this?

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_short_14 <- tenders |>
      mutate(days_open = as.numeric(as_date(closing) - as_date(published))) |>
      filter(days_open < 14) |>
      select(tender_id, org, days_open)
    ex_short_14
    ```
    Even with the shorter norm, `r nrow(ex_short_14)` tenders fall short, both of the PWD, Amarpur Division. `r ex_short_14$tender_id[1]` was open for `r ex_short_14$days_open[1]` days and `r ex_short_14$tender_id[2]` for `r ex_short_14$days_open[2]` days. Windows this short need a recorded reason, such as a real emergency.
    :::

2.  **Tenders of each department.** From `tenders`, count the tenders of each organisation on the portal, and find their total value in ₹ lakh.

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_by_org <- tenders |>
      summarise(tenders = n(), value_lakh = round(sum(value) / 1e5, 2), .by = org) |>
      arrange(desc(tenders))
    ex_by_org
    ```
    The portal lists tenders of `r nrow(ex_by_org)` organisations. `r ex_by_org$org[1]` has the most, `r ex_by_org$tenders[1]`. A count like this, compared with the department's own figures, is a quick test that the scrape covered what we expected.
    :::

3.  **The other direction.** In the chapter we looked for tenders in the register that the portal does not show. Now look the other way. Does the portal show any tender of the PWD, Amarpur Division that is missing from the division's register?

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_not_in_register <- tenders |>
      filter(org == "PWD, Amarpur Division") |>
      anti_join(tender_register, by = "tender_id")
    ex_not_in_register
    ```
    The result has `r nrow(ex_not_in_register)` rows. Every tender of the division on the portal is in its register. A tender published but left out of the register would have been a finding too, so the check is worth making both ways.
    :::

4.  **Competition for the awarded works.** From `awards`, find the awards that received fewer than three bids, with the firm and the value.

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_few_bids <- awards |>
      filter(bids < 3) |>
      select(tender_id, bids, awarded_to, portal_value)
    ex_few_bids
    ```
    `r ex_few_bids$tender_id` received only `r ex_few_bids$bids` bids, and was awarded to `r ex_few_bids$awarded_to` for ₹`r inr(ex_few_bids$portal_value)`. Few bids suggest weak competition. The auditor would see how long the tender was open, and how widely it was advertised.
    :::

5.  **Payments after debarment ended.** Using the cleaned names, list any payment made to a firm after its debarment had ended. These are not findings, but the auditor should note them.

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_after <- payments |>
      inner_join(debarred, by = "name_key") |>
      filter(payment_date > to) |>
      select(voucher_no, payment_date, payee, amount, to)
    ex_after
    ```
    `r ex_after$payee` was paid ₹`r inr(ex_after$amount)` on `r format(ex_after$payment_date, "%d %B %Y")`, after its debarment ended on `r format(ex_after$to, "%d %B %Y")`. The payment is in order, but a firm once debarred deserves care in later contracts.
    :::

## Summary of functions used

| Function | Package | What it does |
|-----------------------|----------------|--------------------------------|
| `read_html()` | rvest | Reads a web page from a file or a web address |
| `minimal_html()` | rvest | Makes a page from a piece of HTML in a string, for practice |
| `html_elements()` | rvest | Selects all elements matching a CSS selector |
| `html_element()` | rvest | Selects the first matching element, one for each input, `NA` if none |
| `html_text2()` | rvest | Text of elements, as the browser shows it |
| `html_attr()` | rvest | Value of an attribute, such as the `href` of a link |
| `html_table()` | rvest | Reads an HTML table into a tibble |
| `url_absolute()` | rvest | Turns a relative link into a full address |
| `write_html()` | xml2 | Writes a parsed page back to a file |
| `map()`, `list_rbind()` | purrr | Read many pages and stack the results |
| `dmy_hm()`, `dmy()`, `as_date()` | lubridate | Read dates written day first, and drop the time |
| `parse_number()` | readr | Turns text like "₹ 1,24,50,000.00" into a number |
| `pivot_wider()` | tidyr | Turns a label and value table into one row |
| `inner_join()`, `anti_join()`, `cross_join()` | dplyr | Compare scraped data with the auditee's records |
| `str_to_upper()`, `str_remove_all()`, `str_replace_all()`, `str_squish()` | stringr | Clean firm names before matching |
| `stringdist()` | stringdist | Distance between two names, for fuzzy matching |
| `md5sum()` | tools | Checksum of a file, to show it has not changed |
| `request()`, `req_user_agent()`, `req_throttle()`, `req_retry()`, `req_perform()` | httr2 | Polite requests to a real website (not run here) |
